entities.name: Anabasis
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Anabasis is the most famous work of the Ancient Greek professional soldier and writer Xenophon. It gives an account of the expedition of the Ten Thousand, an army of Greek mercenaries hired by Cyrus the Younger to help him seize the throne of Persia from his brother, Artaxerxes II, in 401 BC.


The expedition, which began in 401 BC, followed a grueling 12-year journey across Persia, with the Greek mercenaries facing numerous challenges and battles against the Persian army. The expedition ended in defeat at the Battle of Cunaxa in 401 BC, where Cyrus the Younger was killed, and the survivors were forced to march back to Greece with minimal supplies.


Despite the initial failure, the expedition's legacy lived on, and Xenophon's account of the journey, Anabasis, became a classic of ancient Greek literature, providing valuable insights into the culture, politics, and military tactics of the ancient world.


Anabasis also had significant cultural and intellectual impacts, influencing the development of Western literature and military strategy, and serving as a model for later historical accounts and literary works.


The expedition's survival against incredible odds also reflects the resilience and adaptability of the Greek mercenaries, who faced not only military challenges but also cultural and linguistic barriers as they navigated the vast and complex Persian Empire.


The journey of the Ten Thousand remains one of the most famous and enduring stories of ancient Greek military history, a testament to the bravery, determination, and cultural exchange that characterized the ancient world.
